The misguided, by contrast, have received the opposites of these three: being lost from the path of felicity, falling into the opposite of mercy—pain and punishment—and blame and curse, which is the opposite of blessing.

Since each servant's share of mercy is according to his share of guidance, the most perfect of believers in faith is the greatest of them in mercy, as God says about the companions of His Messenger ﷺ: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

Al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him) was among the most merciful of this community. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The most merciful of my community toward my community is Abu Bakr." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi. He was also the most knowledgeable of the Companions by the consensus of the Companions, as Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was the most knowledgeable of us about him"—meaning the Prophet ﷺ. Thus God combined for him breadth of knowledge and mercy.

So it is with a man: as his knowledge expands, his mercy expands. Our Lord has encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge: His mercy has encompassed all things, and He has comprehended all things in knowledge. He is more merciful to His servants than a mother to her child, indeed He is more merciful to the servant than the servant is to himself, just as He is more knowledgeable of the servant's welfare than the servant himself. The servant, out of his ignorance of his own welfare and his wronging of himself, strives for what harms and pains him, diminishes his share of God's honor and reward, and distances himself from God's nearness, while he thinks he is benefiting and honoring himself. This is the extreme of ignorance and injustice, and "man is wrongdoing and ignorant." How many a person honors himself in his own estimation while he is humiliating himself; pampers himself while he is wearing himself out; gives himself some of what he desires and pleasure while barring himself from all its true delights. He has no knowledge of the welfare that is truly its welfare, and no mercy toward it. So his enemy does not inflict on him what he inflicts on himself. He has cheated himself of its share, wasted its right, neglected its welfare, and sold its lasting bliss and complete, enduring pleasure for a fleeting pleasure mixed with disturbance—it is only like confused dreams or a phantom that visits in sleep. This is not strange from such a person, for he has lost his share of guidance and mercy. Had he been guided and shown mercy, his condition would be other than this. But the Lord, exalted is He, knows best the place fit for guidance and mercy. He is the One who bestows them upon the servant, as He said of His servant al-Khidr: ﴿So they found a servant of Our servants, to whom We had given mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾ [al-Kahf: 65], and ﴿Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair﴾ [al-Kahf: 10].

It should be known that mercy is an attribute that entails conveying benefits and welfare to the servant, even if his soul dislikes it and finds it hard. This is true mercy. So the most merciful of people toward you is the one who is hard on you in conveying your welfare and warding off harms from you.

Of the father's mercy toward his child is that he compels him to discipline himself with knowledge and action, is hard on him in that by beating him and otherwise, and prevents him from desires that would return to his harm. Whenever he neglects his child, it is due to the weakness of his mercy toward him, even if he thinks he is being merciful [and indulging him and giving him ease]. This is mercy accompanied by ignorance, like the mercy of a mother.

For this reason, among the perfection of the mercy of the Most Merciful of the merciful is the imposition of various kinds of trial upon the servant, for He knows his welfare better. So His testing him, examining him, and preventing him from many of his desires and appetites is part of His mercy toward him. But the servant, out of his ignorance and wrongdoing, accuses his Lord because of the trial, and does not recognize His kindness to him through that trial and examination.

(Benefit)
Know that when the servant considers what he is in of subtle kindnesses and witnesses them as pure favor and sheer generosity, he also witnesses his poverty toward Him at every moment and his complete lack of independence from Him for the blink of an eye. This is among the greatest doors of gratitude, causes of increase, and the continual flow of blessings upon him.

Whenever blessings follow upon him, they produce in his heart clouds of joy. When these clouds spread across the sky of his heart and his horizon is filled with them, they rain upon him a heavy downpour of delight, by what he is in of sweet happiness. If no heavy rain reaches him, then a light drizzle does. At that time there flows upon his tongue and outwardly a river of boasting, without self-admiration or pride, but out of joy in the bounty and mercy of God, as God said: ﴿Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. So the boasting is outward, while need and humility are inward, and neither negates the other.

Reflect on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without boasting." How he informed of God's bounty and favor upon him; and he informed that this did not proceed from him out of boasting over those beneath him, but rather to manifest God's blessing upon him and to inform the community of the rank of their imam and leader before God and the elevation of his station with Him, so that the community might know God's blessing upon him and upon them.

This resembles the saying of Joseph the Truthful to the ruler: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 55]. His telling of himself this, since it included a benefit returning to the ruler, to the community, and to himself, was good; for he did not intend by it to boast over them. The source of the statement and what motivates it make it good or bad, though its outward form is the same.

(Another benefit)
Joy in His bounty and mercy follows from joy in Him, glorified is He.

The believer rejoices in his Lord more greatly than anyone rejoices in what they delight in: a beloved, a life, wealth, a blessing, or a kingdom. The believer rejoices in his Lord more than all of this. The heart does not attain the true reality of life until it finds the taste of this joy and delight, so that its gladness shows in the heart and its radiance in the face, and it comes to share in the condition of the people of Paradise, to whom God gave radiance and joy.

For such a thing let those who work strive, and in this let the competitors compete. This is the knowledge toward which people of high aspiration and resolve have pressed, and to which the possessors of distinction and nobility have raced.

﻿"Those are the noble qualities, not two cups of milk mixed with water—so what comes after the dregs?"

(Section)
His saying: "...what produces joy, except what is mixed with fear of deception."

That is: this glance from the servant produces joy for him when he knows that his Lord's bounty has preceded him in this before He created him, along with His knowledge of him, his conditions, and his shortcomings in detail. His knowledge of him did not prevent Him from decreeing that bounty and kindness for him. He knows him fully since He originated him from the earth and while he was a fetus in his mother's womb. Yet He decreed for him bounty and generosity without any cause from him, even though He knows that there will come from causes what necessitates cutting that off and withholding it from him.

When the servant witnesses this, his joy in his Lord and in the places of His bounty and kindness intensifies. This is praiseworthy joy, not blameworthy. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate﴾ [Yunus: 58].

His bounty is Islam and faith; His mercy is knowledge and the Qur'an. He loves that His servant rejoice in this and be gladdened by it. Indeed, He loves that His servant rejoice in a good deed when he performs it and be gladdened by it. In reality, this is joy in God's bounty, since God granted him success in it, helped him to it, and made it easy for him. So in truth the servant only rejoices in God's bounty and mercy.

Among the greatest stations of faith is joy in God and gladness in Him. He rejoices in Him as his servant and lover, and as Lord and God, Benefactor and Nurturer, far more than a servant rejoices in a created master who is compassionate toward him, able to grant what the servant wants and seeks from him, and varied in his kindness toward him and in defending him.

His saying "...except what is mixed with fear of deception": that is, what mingles with it. Joy and gladness expand the soul and make it grow, and cause it to forget its faults, afflictions and defects; for if it witnessed these and saw them, they would preoccupy it away from joy.

Also, joy in a blessing may cause one to forget the Giver, so that he busies himself with the robe He has bestowed upon him and turns away from Him. Then gladness overflows upon him until he is absorbed in His blessing and loses sight of Him. Here deception is nearer to him than the hand is to the mouth.

How many there are here who take back from him what He gave him, out of His might and wisdom! Perhaps that is itself mercy toward him, for had he continued in that favor, he would have been in danger of transgression, as God said: ﴿No indeed! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6-7]. If this is the self-sufficiency of perishable worldly property, how about self-sufficiency in what is higher than that and greater? The possessor of this, if the fear of deception does not accompany him, is in danger of having it taken from him and being brought low.

The "deception" he is feared to fall into is that God, glorified is He, hides from him the witnessing of his original dependence in that, of His favor and bounty, that it is pure bounty from Him upon him, and that it is by Him alone and from Him alone. Thus he loses sight of the reality of His words: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]; His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, the affair is entirely Allah's﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]; and His words: ﴿And if Allah touches you with adversity, there is no remover of it but He; and if He intends for you good, then there is no repeller of His bounty; He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [Yunus: 107];

and His words: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be delivered to you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 86]; and His words: ﴿And were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, not one of you would ever have been purified; but Allah purifies whom He wills﴾ [al-Nur: 21]; and similar verses.

So He hides him from witnessing these, and refers him to his own knowledge in his earning and seeking. He refers him to his own self, which has poverty essentially, and veils him from being referred to the wealthy, faithful One who possesses complete independence essentially. This is among the greatest causes of deception. And God is the One sought for help.

No matter how far the servant attains in obedience, he should never be free of this caution. The best of His creation and the choicest of His servants feared it. Shu'ayb (upon him peace), when his people said to him: ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you from our town, or you will return to our religion.' He said: 'Even if we were unwilling?' 'We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], up to His words: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾ [al-A'raf: 89]—he referred the matter to the will and knowledge of God, Exalted, out of good manners with God, knowledge of the right of Lordship, and standing within the limit of servanthood. Likewise Abraham (upon him peace) said to his people, when they frightened him with their idols: ﴿And I do not fear that which you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [al-An'am: 80]; he referred the matter to God's will and knowledge. And God, Exalted, said: ﴿Then do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people﴾ [al-A'raf: 99].

(Admonition)
When people are content with the world, be content with Allah. When they rejoice in the world, rejoice in Allah. When they find comfort in their loved ones, make your comfort in Allah. When they seek acquaintance with their kings and great ones and draw near to them to gain honor and elevation through them, then seek acquaintance with Allah and draw near to Him; by that you will attain the utmost of might and elevation.

Some ascetics said: "I know of no one who has heard of Paradise and Hell and passed a single hour without disobeying God in it, except one who remembered, prayed, recited, or did good." A man said to him: "I weep a great deal." He said: "If you laugh while acknowledging your sin is better than that you weep while relying on your deeds, for one who relies on his deeds, his deeds do not rise above his head." The man said: "Advise me." He said: "Leave the world to its people as they left the Hereafter to its people, and be in this world like the bee: if it eats, it eats what is good; if it feeds, it feeds what is good; and if it lands on something, it does not break it or scratch it."

[Section: The Station of Joy]
Said the author of "al-Manazil":

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 10, verse 58 (part 3 of 3)**

**Chapter on Joy (al-Surur).** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice. It is better than what they accumulate."﴾ [Yunus: 58].

Opening the chapter with this verse is most fitting. Allah the Exalted commanded His servants to rejoice in His bounty (fadl) and His mercy (rahmah). This follows from rejoicing in and being glad of the One who possesses bounty and mercy. For whoever rejoices in what reaches him from a generous, benevolent, and kind benefactor, his joy in the One who delivered it to him is more fitting and more deserving.

We will mention the meaning of this verse, and then explain the words of the author (al-Musannif).

Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and others said: "The bounty of Allah is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an." They made His mercy more specific than His bounty, since His particular bounty is general to the people of Islam, while His mercy is through teaching His Book to some of them and not others. He made them Muslims by His bounty, and He sent down His Book to them by His mercy. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be delivered to you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qasas: 86].

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made us among its people."

I say: He means by this that there are two matters here.

The first is the bounty in itself. The second is the readiness of the recipient to accept it, like rain that falls upon land that is receptive to plant growth. Thus the intended purpose is accomplished through the bounty and the receptacle's acceptance of it. And Allah knows best.

Joy (al-farah) is a pleasure that enters the heart upon perceiving the beloved and attaining the desired. From its perception there arises a state called joy and gladness (al-surur), just as sorrow and grief arise from the loss of the beloved. When one loses it, a state called sorrow and grief arises from its loss. Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the command to rejoice in His bounty and mercy directly after His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [Yunus: 57].

Nothing is more deserving that a servant rejoice in than the bounty and mercy of Allah, which include the admonition and the healing of the breasts from their diseases through guidance and mercy. Allah, glorified is He, informed us that what He gave His servants of admonition, which is the command and prohibition joined with encouragement and warning, and the healing of the breasts that includes their well-being from the disease of ignorance, darkness, error, and foolishness, is more painful to them than the diseases of the body. However, because the breasts have become accustomed to these diseases, they do not feel their pain. Their sense of them only grows strong at the moment of departing this world. There, every painful and grievous thing comes to them. What their Lord gave them is the guidance which includes the coolness of the breasts through certainty, the tranquility of the heart in it, the calm of the soul in it, and the life of the spirit through it, as well as the mercy which brings them every good and pleasure, and repels from them every evil and painful thing.

That is better than everything people accumulate of the goods and adornments of this world. That is, this is what should be rejoiced in. Whoever rejoices in it has rejoiced in the most excellent thing to rejoice in, not in what the people of this world accumulate from it, for it is not a proper object of joy, because it is exposed to calamities, quick to vanish, of grave outcome, and it is like the phantom of a dream that visits the lovesick one in sleep. Then the sleep ends, the phantom departs, and its visit is followed by separation.

Joy appears in the Qur'an in two forms: absolute (mutlaq) and restricted (muqayyad).

The absolute form appears in a context of blame, such as His saying: ﴿Do not rejoice; indeed, Allah does not like those who rejoice﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10].

The restricted form is also of two kinds. One is restricted to the worldly life, which makes its possessor forget the bounty and favor of Allah, and this is blameworthy, as in His saying: ﴿Until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

The second is restricted to the bounty and mercy of Allah, which is also of two kinds: bounty and mercy by way of cause (al-sabab), and bounty and mercy by way of effect (al-musabbab). The first is like His saying: ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice. It is better than what they accumulate."﴾ [Yunus: 58]. The second is like His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170].

Rejoicing in Allah, His Messenger, faith, the Sunnah, knowledge, and the Qur'an is among the highest stations of the knowers of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]. And He said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book rejoice in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 36].

Rejoicing in knowledge, faith, and the Sunnah is evidence of esteeming them in the heart of their possessor, loving them, and preferring them over other things. For a servant's joy in a thing upon attaining it is according to the measure of his love for it and his desire for it. Whoever has no desire for a thing, its attainment does not bring him joy, nor does its loss bring him grief.

So joy follows love and desire.

The difference between it and good tidings (al-istibshar) is that joy is in the beloved after it has been attained, while good tidings can occur before attaining it when one is confident of its attainment. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty and receiving good tidings concerning those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170].

Joy is an attribute of perfection, and for this reason the Lord, the Exalted, is described with its highest and most perfect forms. Like His joy at the repentance of the one who repents, which is greater than the joy of the one who finds his riding beast, upon which were his food and drink, in a deadly desert after having lost it and despaired of recovering it.

The point is that joy is the highest of the kinds of the heart's bliss, its pleasure, and its radiance. Joy and gladness are its delight, and worry and grief are its torment. Joy in a thing is above contentment (al-ridha) with it, for contentment is tranquility, calm, and expansion of the breast, while joy is pleasure, radiance, and gladness. So every joyful person is content, but not every content person is joyful. For this reason joy is the opposite of grief, and contentment is the opposite of wrath (al-sukht). Grief pains its possessor, while wrath does not pain him, except when accompanied by inability to take revenge. And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Definition of Gladness (al-Surur)]

The author of al-Manazil (Sahib al-Manazil) said:

Gladness (al-surur) is a name for a comprehensive good tidings. It is purer than joy, because joys are sometimes mixed with sorrows. For this reason the Qur'an has descended using its name for the joys of this world in several places, and the word gladness appears in two places in the Qur'an in the context of the Hereafter.

Gladness (al-surur) and delight (al-masarrah) are the verbal noun of sarrahu surūran wa masarrah (he gladdened him). It seems that the meaning of sarrahu is: he affected the creases (asarir) of his face, for the creases of the face shine from it. As the poet of the Arabs said:

*And when you look at the creases of his face,*
*they shine like the flash of a bright, gleaming cloud.*

This is like how one says: "rasahu" (he struck his head) if he struck his head, "batanahu" and "zahrahu" if he struck his belly and back, and "ammahu" if he struck the crown of his head.

As for good tidings (al-istibshar), it is the form istif'al from al-bushra (good news). The bishara (glad tiding) is the first truthful news that brings joy.

The word al-bushra (good tidings) is used to mean two things. One is the glad tiding of the one who informs. The other is the gladness of the one who is informed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For them are good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64]. The word al-bushra has been explained in both senses. In the hadith of Ubadah ibn al-Samit and Abu al-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is the true dream that a Muslim sees, or that is seen for him."

Ibn Abbas said: "The good tidings of the life of this world are at death, when the angels of mercy come to them with good tidings from Allah. And in the Hereafter, at the departure of the soul of the believer, when they ascend with it to Allah, it is escorted as a bride is escorted, and it is given good tidings of the pleasure of Allah."

Al-Hasan said: "It is Paradise." This was chosen by al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'. The good tidings of this world were explained as a good reputation that is spoken of on people's tongues. All of this is correct.

So praise is one of the good tidings, the true dream is one of the good tidings, the angels' glad tidings to him at death is one of the good tidings, and Paradise is among the greatest good tidings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believed and did righteous deeds that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25]. And He said: ﴿And receive good tidings of the Paradise which you were promised﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

It is said that it was named so because it affects the skin of the face (bashrat al-wajh). For this reason it has two kinds: a glad good tiding, which affects the face with radiance and delight, and a grievous good tiding, which affects it with dejection and frowning. But when it is used without restriction, it means gladness. When it is restricted, it takes the meaning to which it is restricted.

His words "and it is purer than joy" are supported by the argument that joys are sometimes mixed with sorrows, meaning that their opposite is sometimes blended with them. This is unlike gladness.

It is said: Delights are also sometimes mixed with distresses and sorrows, so there is no difference.

His words: "For this reason the Qur'an has descended using its name for the joys of this world in several places," means that Allah the Exalted attributed joy to the conditions of this world in His saying: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-An'am: 44], in His saying: ﴿Do not rejoice; indeed, Allah does not like those who rejoice﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10]. For the joys of this world are never entirely free of sorrows and griefs. Rather, there is no joy without a grief preceding it, accompanying it, or following it. Joy is never unmixed; there must be a grief accompanying it. But sometimes joy overcomes sorrow, so its ruling and pain are overwhelmed while joy exists, and vice versa.

It is said: The Qur'an has also descended with joy regarding the matters of the Hereafter in several places, such as His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170], and His saying: ﴿In that let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. So there is no difference between them from this aspect that he mentioned.

His words: "And the name gladness (al-surur) appears in the Qur'an in two places in the context of the Hereafter."

He means by them His saying: ﴿As for he who is given his record in his right hand, he will be judged with an easy account and will return to his family joyful﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 7-9]. The second place is His saying: ﴿And He will give them radiance and gladness﴾ [al-Insan: 11].

It is said: Gladness has appeared regarding the conditions of this world in one place in a blameworthy manner, such as His saying: ﴿But as for he who is given his record behind his back, he will call for destruction and will enter the Blaze. Indeed, he was among his people, joyful﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 10-13].

So you have seen that each of joy and gladness occurs in the Qur'an with reference to the conditions of this world and the conditions of the Hereafter. Therefore the preference the author mentioned does not clearly appear.

Indeed, it may be said that joy is preferred, because the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, is described with it, and His name is applied to Him, not gladness. This indicates that its meaning is more perfect than the meaning of gladness. Allah commanded it in His saying: ﴿In that let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58], and praised the blessed for it in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170].

As for His saying: ﴿And He will give them radiance and gladness﴾ [al-Insan: 11], and His saying: ﴿and he will return to his family joyful﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 9], here He turned to the word gladness for the agreement of the verse endings (ru'us al-ayy). Had he titled the chapter "The Chapter on Joy," it would have matched more exactly the verse he cited as evidence. But the matter is minor, and the intended purpose lies beyond that.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 10, verse 61:

As for the placing of the earth before the heavens in Surah Yunus, since the context is one of warning and threat to mankind, and of informing them that He (glorified be He) knows their deeds, both the minute and the grand, and that nothing of them is hidden from Him, this required mentioning their place, which is the earth, before mentioning the heavens. Blessed is He who deposited in His speech such wisdom, secrets and sciences as bear witness that it is the speech of God Most High, and that no created being could ever produce the like of this wisdom.

Ibn al-Qayyim also said:

As for the placing of the earth first in His words, ﴿Nor is hidden from your Lord the weight of an atom's [particle] within the earth or within the heaven﴾, it is also due to rank, since it is linked to the mention of what is nearer to Him, namely those addressed in His words, ﴿nor do you do any deed﴾. The beauty of the arrangement therefore required placing the earth first in mention, together with the addressees who are its inhabitants, unlike the verse in Saba', which is linked to His words ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾.

As for His placing of wealth before children in many verses, it is because children, once wealth exists, are a blessing and a joy, whereas in times of poverty and bad condition they are a worry and a harm. This is therefore from the category of placing the cause before the effect, since wealth is the complete cause of the blessing of children.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 10, verse 85:

The companions of Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.﴾

Mujahid said: The meaning is: do not punish us at their hands, nor with a punishment from You, so that they would say, "If these were upon the truth, this would not have befallen them."

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: its meaning is: do not let them prevail over us, so that they would think they are upon the truth, and thus be tempted by that.

Al-Farra' said: Do not let the disbelievers prevail over us, so that they would see that they are upon the truth and that we are upon falsehood.

Muqatil said: Do not restrict our provision and expand it for them, for that would be a trial for them.

It is among the finest and most masterful arrangements (nazm) of speech. He first used the dual, because Musa and Harun were the two messengers whose commands were to be obeyed, and it is obligatory upon the Children of Israel to obey each of them equally. And when they settled homes for their people, the people follow them. Then He used the plural pronoun, saying: ﴿And establish prayer﴾, because establishing it is an obligation upon all. Then He used the singular in His saying: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾, indicating that Musa is the origin of the prophethood and his brother was a supporter and minister. Just as they were sent with one message, they were one messenger, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾. So this messenger is the one who was told: ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾..

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 10, verse 94:

This verse has caused confusion for many people, and the Jews and Christians raised an objection against the Muslims concerning it. They said: "He was in doubt, so he was commanded to ask us." Yet, praise be to God, there is no difficulty in it. The objection arises only from the bad intention and the lack of understanding of those who raise it, the likes of cattle. Otherwise, the verse is among the signs of his prophethood ﷺ. Nothing in the verse indicates that doubt occurred, or that asking occurred at all. For a conditional clause does not indicate that the condition has occurred, nor even that it is possible, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya' 22], and His saying: ﴿Say: Had there been with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra' 42], and His saying: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshipers﴾ [al-Zukhruf 81], and His saying: ﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you and to those before you: If you should associate others with God, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar 65], and their like. The Messenger of God ﷺ never doubted and never asked.

In the tafsir of Sa'id, on the authority of Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'I do not doubt, and I do not ask.'"

Ibn Juraij related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "If you are in doubt that you are written down with them, then ask them." This is the view chosen by Ibn Jarir.

He said: God, the Exalted, says to His Prophet: "If you, O Muhammad, are in doubt about the truth of what We have informed you and sent down to you, namely that the Children of Israel did not differ concerning your prophethood before I sent you as a messenger to My creation, for they find you written down with them and recognise you by the attribute with which you are described in their books, then ask those who read the Book before you, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and others like him among the people of truth and faith in you from among them, not the people of lying and disbelief in you."

Likewise Ibn Zayd said: "He is 'Abdullah ibn Salam, who was among the People of the Book and then believed in the Messenger of God ﷺ."

Al-Dahhak said: "Ask the people of piety and faith among the believers of the People of the Book, those who met the Prophet of God ﷺ."

But neither of these views conforms to the meaning and intent of the verse. Where was 'Abdullah ibn Salam at the time this verse was revealed? The surah is Meccan, and Ibn Salam at that time was upon the religion of his people. And how could the Messenger of God ﷺ be commanded to call upon his followers as witnesses against those who denied his prophethood?

Many exegetes said: "This address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but what is meant is others, because the Qur'an was revealed to him in the language of the Arabs, and they sometimes address a man with something while meaning someone else, as their proverb-maker says: '(It is you I mean, but listen, O neighbour).'"

Like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, fear God and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab 1], where what is meant by this address is his followers.

Abu Ishaq said: God, the Exalted, addresses the Prophet ﷺ, but the address is general to all creation, and the meaning is: "And if you are in doubt..." The evidence for this is His saying at the end of the surah: ﴿Say: O people, if you are in doubt about my religion, then I do not worship those whom you worship besides God﴾ [Yunus 104].

Ibn Qutaybah said: At the time of the Prophet ﷺ people were of several kinds: one who disbelieved in him and denied him, another who believed in him and affirmed him, and another who was in doubt about the matter, not knowing what it was, moving one foot forward and one foot back. God, the Exalted, addressed this category of people and said: "If you, O human being, are in doubt about what We have sent down to you of guidance upon the tongue of Muhammad, then ask."

He said: He used the singular while meaning the plural, as He said: ﴿O human being, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ [al-Infitar 6], and: ﴿O human being, indeed you are labouring toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾ [al-Inshiqaq 6], and: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾ [al-Zumar 8].

This view, though it has some basis, is contradicted by the context of the discourse, so reflect upon it.

Consider also His saying: ﴿those who read the Book before you﴾ [Yunus 94], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ [Yunus 96], and His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus 99]. All of this is one continuous address, each part connected to the next.

When the proponents of this view realised that the address could only be directed to the Prophet ﷺ, they said: "The address is to him, but what is meant is this category of doubters." All of this is a flight from imagining what is not imagined: that doubt or asking occurred from him. We have already shown that this does not even entail that it is possible, let alone that it occurred.

If it is said: Then if it has not occurred and is not possible, what is the intended purpose of the address and what is meant by it?

It is said: Its purpose is to establish proof against those who deny prophethoods and monotheism, and that they acknowledge this and do not reject or deny it, and that God, glorified be He, sent His messengers to them and sent down His books to them with this, and sent His angels to His prophets with His revelation and speech. So whoever doubts this, let him ask the People of the Book. Thus this meaning is expressed in the most concise phrasing and the clearest in indicating the intent, by addressing His Messenger, who never doubted and never asked, and nothing ever arose to necessitate that. And when you reflect upon this address, there appears to you on its very surface: whoever doubts, let him ask; My Messenger never doubted and never asked.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 10, verse 99–100:

The intended meaning is that faith is attained by all of them, not that all of them believe at one and the same time, the earliest of them and the latest of them.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah, and He places defilement upon those who do not reason﴾

His permission here means His decree and His predestination, not merely His command and His legislation. Thus did the early scholars (al-salaf) explain this verse. Ibn al-Mubarak related from al-Thawri: "By the decree of Allah."

And Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: "He, dhikruhu jall (may His remembrance be exalted), says to His Prophet: 'And no soul was created with a path to believe you unless He permits it to do so. So do not exert yourself in seeking its guidance, deliver to it the warning of Allah, then leave it, for its guidance is in the hand of its Creator.'" What comes before and after the verse indicates nothing but this, for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers? And it is not for a soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: your call alone is not sufficient for faith to occur until Allah permits those you call to believe. Then He said: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾

Ibn Jarir said: He, exalted is He, says: O Muhammad, say to these who ask you for signs confirming what you call to, the tawhid of Allah and the renunciation of rivals and idols: Look, O people, at what is in the heavens of signs indicating the truth of what I call you to, the tawhid of Allah, from its sun and its moon, the alternation of its night and its day, and the descent of rain bringing the provision of the servants from its clouds; and in the earth, from its mountains, its splitting open with its plants, the sustenance of its inhabitants, and all kinds of its wonders. For in that is, for you, if you reason and reflect, an admonition and a lesson, and an indication that this is the work of One who cannot have a partner in His dominion, nor a helper in its preservation and governance, who suffices you from anything else of the signs. But signs avail not a people for whom wretchedness has already been decreed by Allah and judged against them in the Mother of the Book, that they are among the people of the Fire. They do not believe in any of that, nor do they affirm it, even if every sign came to them, until they see the painful punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 10, verse 107:

The created being has no power to benefit or harm the servant, nor to give or withhold. Rather, it is his Lord, glory be to Him, who created him, provided for him, gave him sight, guided him, bestowed upon him blessings in abundance, and showed love to him through them, while He is free of need of him, and while the servant displeases Him through acts of disobedience, despite the servant's neediness toward Him. So when Allah afflicts him with harm, there is none to remove it but Him, and when He bestows upon him His blessings, there is none to turn them back or withhold them, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If Allah touches you with adversity, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He intends for you good, there is none to repel His bounty. He causes it to reach whom He wills of His servants, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [Yunus: 107], and ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to the people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him. And He is the Almighty, the Wise﴾ [Fatir: 2]. Thus the servant does not benefit, harm, give, or withhold except by the permission of Allah. The affair is entirely Allah's, first and last, outward and inward. He is the Turner of hearts and the Director of them as He wills, the One alone who holds harm and benefit, giving and withholding, lowering and raising. ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾, ﴿Surely, to Him belong creation and command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

This aspect is greater for the general public than the first aspect, and for this reason they were addressed with it in the Qur'an more than the first. However, whoever reflects upon the method of the Qur'an will realize that Allah, glory be to Him, calls His servants through this aspect to the first. This aspect necessitates reliance upon Allah, seeking His help, supplicating to Him, and asking Him alone, to the exclusion of anything else. It also necessitates loving Him and worshipping Him, because of His goodness to His servant and the abundance of His blessings upon him. So when he worships Him, loves Him, and relies upon Him from this aspect, he enters into the first aspect. Likewise, one who is struck by a great trial and severe poverty or an unsettling fear, and begins to call upon Allah and humble himself before Him, until He opens for him, through the sweetness of intimate conversation with Him, the door of faith in Him and turning to Him, and what is more beloved to Him than that need which he initially intended, while he did not know this at first until he sought it and yearned for it. So He made him know it through the means He established that led him to it. The Qur'an is filled with mention of the servants' need of Allah alone to the exclusion of anything else, and with mention of His blessings upon them, and with mention of what He has promised them in the Hereafter of kinds of bliss and pleasures, and none of this is found with the created being. So this aspect realizes reliance upon Allah, gratitude to Him, and love for Him because of His goodness.

Among what clarifies and strengthens this is that attachment of the servant to other than Allah is harmful to him if he takes from it an amount beyond his need that helps him in the worship of Allah, His love, and the emptying of his heart for Him. If he obtains food and drink beyond his needs, it harms him or destroys him; likewise with marriage and clothing. If he loves something to the extent that he becomes close friends with it, he will inevitably tire of it or part from it. So harm befalls him whether he finds it or loses it: if he loses it, he is tormented and pained by the separation; if he finds it, he suffers more pain than the pleasure he gains. This is a matter known through reflection and induction: whoever loves something other than Allah, for other than Allah, his harm is greater than his benefit and his torment greater than his bliss. What further clarifies this is that his reliance upon the created being and his trust in it necessitate harm to him from that direction, for he will be forsaken from that direction. This is also known through reflection and induction: a servant who attaches his hope and trust to other than Allah will certainly be disappointed from that direction, and whoever seeks help from other than Him will certainly be forsaken. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they might be for them a source of might. No! They will deny their worship of them and will be against them opponents﴾ [Maryam: 81-82], and He said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that perhaps they might be helped. They are not able to help them, and they are for them a mobilized army﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74-75].

And Allah, the Exalted, said about the Imam of the monotheists (Ibrahim), that he said to the polytheists: ﴿You have taken idols besides Allah only as an affection among yourselves in the worldly life; then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others﴾ [al-Ankabut: 25]. And since the ultimate well-being of the servant lies in worshipping Allah alone and seeking help from Him alone, his worship of other than Him and seeking help from other than Him is the ultimate of his harm. Among what further clarifies and explains this matter is that Allah, glory be to Him, is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy, Generous, and Merciful. He is good to His servant despite being free of need of him, desiring good for him and removing harm from him, not to bring any benefit to Himself, nor to repel any harm, but out of mercy, goodness, and pure generosity. He is Merciful by His essence, Benevolent by His essence, Bountiful by His essence, and Generous by His essence, just as He is Self-Sufficient by His essence, Powerful by His essence, and Living by His essence. So His goodness, generosity, kindness, and mercy are necessary attributes of His essence, and they cannot be otherwise, just as His standing (by Himself), power, and self-sufficiency are necessary attributes of His essence, and they cannot be otherwise.

As for created beings, it is inconceivable that they should do good except for their own interests. The most that a created being can do for a servant is to love him and honor him in order to bring him benefit and ward off harm from him, and this is by Allah's facilitation and permission to them. So in reality He is the Patron of this blessing, its bestower, and the one who causes it to flow through their hands. Nevertheless, they only do this for their own interests from the servant: when they love him, they seek to attain their purpose from his love, whether they love him for his inner or outer beauty. When they love the prophets and the saints, and seek to meet them, they desire to enjoy seeing them and hearing their speech and the like. Likewise, whoever loves a person for his bravery, leadership, beauty, or generosity wishes to attain his share from that love, and were it not for his enjoyment of it, he would not love it. And if they bring him benefit or ward off harm from him—such as illness or an enemy—even by supplication, they seek a return if the action was not for Allah's sake. Thus the soldiers of kings, the slaves of masters, the hired workers of employers, and the helpers of a chief all strive only to attain their aims through him. Most of them do not turn toward seeking the benefit of their master, unless he has knowledge and discipline from another direction, which then enters into the religious aspect, or unless there is in him a natural disposition of justice and goodness out of reciprocation and mercy. Otherwise, the primary intention is the benefit of himself. This is from the wisdom of Allah by which He establishes the interests of His creation, for He distributed their livelihood among them in the worldly life and raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others in service.

(Section)

For Allah, glory be to Him, over His servant there is a command He commands him with, a decree He decrees upon him, and a blessing He bestows upon him; he is never free of these three.

The decree is of two kinds: either calamities or faults. Over these he has servitude in all these stages. The dearest of creation to Him is the one who knows his servitude in these stages and fulfills its right; this is the nearest of creation to Him. The farthest from Him is the one who is ignorant of his servitude in these stages and neglects it in knowledge and in action. His servitude in the command is to carry it out sincerely and to follow the Messenger of Allah; and in the prohibition, to avoid it out of fear, reverence, and love of Him. His servitude in the decree of calamities is patience upon them, then contentment with them, which is higher than patience, then gratitude for them, which is higher than contentment. This only comes from him when his love has taken firm root in his heart, and he knows the goodness of Allah's choice for him, His kindness and gentleness toward him, and His benevolence to him through the calamity, even if he dislikes the calamity. His servitude in the decree of faults is to hasten to repent from them, to disown them, and to stand in the station of seeking excuse and humility, knowing that none can lift them from him except Him, and none can protect him from their evil besides Him, and that if they continue they will distance him from his Lord and drive him from His door. He sees them as a harm that none but Him can remove, to the point that he regards them as greater than harm to the body. So he seeks refuge in His pleasure from His anger, in His pardon from His punishment, and seeks protection and refuge in Him from Himself, knowing that if He leaves him and leaves him to himself, he will return to the like of them and worse than them, and that he has no way to give them up and repent except through His grace and help, and that this is in the hand of Allah, glory be to Him, not in the hand of the servant. He is weaker, more powerless, and less capable than to guide himself or to bring about the pleasure of his Master without His permission, will, and help. So he is one who takes refuge in Him, humbled, lowly, destitute, casting himself before Him, lying at His door, the most abject and broken of things before Him, the poorest, most in need of Him, most desirous of Him, and most loving of Him. His body moves about his affairs while his heart prostrates before Him. He knows with certainty that there is no good in him, nor from him, nor by him, nor for him; that all good is Allah's and in His hands, by Him and from Him. He is the Patron of his blessings, the One who initiated them for him without any entitlement, and the One who causes them to flow to him, while he is despised by Him for his turning away, heedlessness, and disobedience. So the share of Allah, glory be to Him, is praise, gratitude, and thanks, and the share of the servant is blame, deficiency, and fault. He has monopolized praise and commendation and thanks, and has left the servant with blame and deficiencies and faults. So all praise is for Him, all good is in His hands, all grace is His, all thanks is His, and all favor is His. From Him is the beneficence, and from the servant is the wrongdoing; from Him is the kindness toward the servant through His blessings, and from the servant is the disobedience toward Him through his sins; from Him is the sincere counsel for His servant, and from the servant is the deceit toward Him in his dealings.

As for the servitude of blessings, it is to recognize them and acknowledge them first, then to seek refuge in Him lest their attribution and ascription to other than Him enter the heart, even if it is a means among the means; for He is the Causer of the cause and its Establisher. So the blessing is from Him alone in every respect and consideration. Then comes praising Him for them, loving Him for them, and thanking Him by employing them in His obedience. Among the subtle aspects of worshipping through blessings is to regard their little as much and to consider his great gratitude for them as little, and to know that they reached him from his Master without any price he paid for them, nor any means he used to seek them, nor any entitlement of his to them, and that in reality they belong to Allah, not to the servant. So blessings only increase him in humility, lowliness, modesty, and love of the Benefactor. Every time He renews a blessing for him, he renews for it servitude, love, submission, and lowliness; every time He takes something from him, he renews contentment; every time he commits a sin, he renews repentance, humility, and seeking excuse. This is the shrewd servant, while the incapable one is far from this. And success is from Allah.

(Section)

Al-Sahl said: "Seeking refuge is only upon knowledge of trial," meaning: knowledge of the One who tests is in proportion to the trial. Whoever knows the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "I seek refuge in You from You," and stands by this knowledge through witnessing and taste, and gives it its due of servitude, he is truly poor, and the foundation of true poverty rests on this word. Whoever is granted understanding of the secret of this has understood the secret of Muhammadan poverty. He, glory be to Him, is the One who delivers from His decree by His decree, and He is the One who seeks refuge in Himself from Himself, and He is the One who repels what comes from Him by what comes from Him. So all creation belongs to Him, all command belongs to Him, and all judgment belongs to Him; what He wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. Whatever He wills, no one can turn away except by His will; and whatever He does not will, it is impossible to bring about except by His will. None brings good deeds but Him, none removes evil deeds but Him, none guides to the best deeds and character but Him, and none turns away their evil but Him: ﴿If Allah touches you with adversity, there is none to remove it except Him; and if He intends for you good, there is none to repel His bounty﴾ [Yunus: 107].

Realization of knowledge of this necessitates the soundness of destitution, complete poverty and neediness, and it prevents the servant from seeing his deeds and states and relying upon them, and from departing from the company of servitude into claiming what is not his.

And how could one claim with God a state, a faculty, or a station, when his heart, his will, and his outward and inward movements are in the hand of his Lord and Sovereign, of which he owns none? Rather, they are in the hand of the Turner of hearts and its Director as He wills. So faith in this and realization of it is the order of monotheism, and whenever it is removed from the heart, the order of monotheism unravels. Glory be to Him, who cannot be reached except through Him, who cannot be obeyed except by His will, and whose honor cannot be attained except by obedience to Him, and there is no path to obeying Him except by His grant and help. So the entire matter returns to Him, just as the entire matter began from Him. He is the First and the Last: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾.

Whoever reaches this state falls into the grip of detachment and isolation, and comes near the station of special monotheism. Monotheism has two kinds: general and special, just as prayer has two kinds, remembrance has two kinds, and all acts of nearness are similarly of a special and a general type. The special is that in which the worker expends his sincere counsel and intention so as to perform it in the best and most complete manner; the general is that which is not like this.

All Muslims share in bringing the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and their differing in knowledge of the content of this testimony and in their standing by it inwardly and outwardly is a matter that none can enumerate except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
